source.title_on_document: Long-term impact of ChatGPT-4 on music students' creative and analytical skills: A follow-up study

supplement.where: The document mentions no supplementary material or online appendix. Data are 'available on request from the corresponding author' (p. 17, Data availability).
supplement.holds: Nothing indicated. No arm-level standard deviations, no per-week means, and no baseline comparison table appear in the main text.

paper_design_summary: Seventy-four second-year Bachelor of Music students at a South Korean university were assigned (randomly, at the class level) to a ChatGPT-4 (ChatGPT-4o) supported course (n = 36) or traditional teacher-led instruction (n = 38) for 24 weeks of composition, improvisation, harmonic analysis, transcription, and arranging. Every two weeks students submitted a creative product and an analytical task, which two blinded external assessors scored with a four-dimension, seven-point creativity rubric and a parallel analytical-skills rubric (12 measurement points). The paper compares groups with latent growth models and a MANCOVA adjusted for prior ChatGPT use and Week 1 scores.

studies.label: 24-week classroom intervention: ChatGPT-4 supported vs traditional music instruction

assignment.what_was_assigned: ChatGPT-4 supported instruction (experimental) vs traditional teacher-led instruction without AI (control); assignment conducted at the class level. The number of classes is not stated. The paper also calls the design quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: In the present study, participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups. ... While the random assignment was conducted at the class level (an unavoidable constraint of the institutional timetable)
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1 Design and participants (also abstract p. 1 and p. 5: 'The study adopted a quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test design.')

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT-4 supported)
arms.description: Integrated ChatGPT-4 (ChatGPT-4o) into weekly composition, improvisation, and analysis tasks: generating melodic/harmonic suggestions, drafting programme notes, receiving simulated feedback; encouraged to critically evaluate and adapt AI output.

arms.name: Control (traditional instruction)
arms.description: Equivalent tasks with textbooks, class notes, lectures, handouts, and teacher consultation; feedback solely from the instructor without AI. Same instructor as the experimental group.

participants.exclusions: No post-assignment exclusions or attrition are reported. Of 86 students in the programme, 12 were used in the pilot and did not join the main study. Table 6 lists N = 36 and N = 38; Levene's tests have df (1, 72), consistent with 74 analyzed.
participants.who: Second-year undergraduates in a Bachelor of Music programme, drawn from the cohort of the authors' earlier study (Zhou & Kim, 2024), in which only the AI-supported condition had received structured ChatGPT-supported learning.
participants.quote: Participants were seventy-four second-year undergraduates enrolled in the Bachelor of Music programme at a university in South Korea.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (the paper specifies the newer generation ChatGPT-4o)
ai_tool.how_used: Weekly learning cycle over 24 weeks: AI generated melodic/harmonic and structural ideas, improvisation tasks and stylistic models, corrections and reharmonizations, checks of transcription accuracy, voicing and orchestration suggestions, and simulated feedback; students revised their work with AI feedback (p. 5, Section 3.2; p. 6, Table 1).

task.description: Music coursework: compositions, recorded improvisations, reharmonizations, stylistic reworking of transcribed material, and arrangements (creative products), each with an accompanying analytical task. No 'music composition' category exists in the codebook task list; creative_writing is the nearest code, design_visual and other are alternatives.
task.duration: 24 weeks over two semesters (October 2024 to January 2025; March to June 2025); submissions every two weeks, 12 measurement points

outcomes.name: Creativity rubric score of submitted music products
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric adapted from Webster (2002) and Burnard's (2012) application of the Consensual Assessment Technique; four dimensions on a seven-point scale (originality of musical ideas, overall musical value, inventiveness in development, expressive impact). Two external assessors with expertise in music theory, composition, and creativity research, blinded to identity, group, and timing; discrepancies greater than two points resolved by discussion (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). No inter-rater reliability statistic is reported for the rubric (kappas on p. 7 refer to the interaction-log coding). Analyzed two ways: latent growth model over 12 points (Table 3, Fig. 1) and MANCOVA/ANCOVA with covariates prior ChatGPT use, Week 1 creativity, Week 1 analytical skills (Tables 4-6). The time point or aggregation used as the MANCOVA dependent variable is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Univariate test, Group on Creativity: df1 = 1, df2 = 69, F = 7.216, p = .009, η² = .096 (Table 5). Adjusted means: Experimental 4.71 (Std. Error 0.18, N = 36) vs Control 4.35 (Std. Error 0.17, N = 38) (Table 6). Multivariate Group effect on creativity and analytical combined: Pillai's Trace = .047, F(2, 68) = 3.982, p = .023, η² = .047 (Table 4).
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Results RQ2; p. 11, Table 4; p. 12, Tables 5 and 6

contrasts.reported: Latent growth model, Creativity. Intercept: Experimental Est. 3.281 (Std. Err. 0.043, p < .000) vs Control 3.004 (0.064, p < .000). Slope: Experimental 0.315 (0.006, p < .000) vs Control 0.210 (0.010, p < .000). Estimated per-group, no test of the between-group slope difference is reported. Fig. 1 plots estimated means from about 3.3 to 6.7 (experimental) and 3.0 to 5.3 (control) over weeks 1-12.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Results RQ1; p. 9, Table 3; p. 10, Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Analytical-skills rubric score of submitted analytical tasks
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Not a creativity outcome; recorded because it is analyzed jointly with creativity. Parallel rubric adapted from Biasutti and Frezza (2009) and Bautista et al. (2018); four dimensions on a seven-point scale (accuracy of harmonic and structural labelling, clarity of theoretical justification, depth of reasoning, transferability of reasoning). Same blinded assessors.

contrasts.reported: Univariate Group on Analytical: F(1, 69) = 5.482, p = .022, η² = .075 (Table 5). Adjusted means: Experimental 4.67 (Std. Error 0.16, N = 36) vs Control 4.38 (0.16, N = 38) (Table 6). Latent growth: intercept 2.973 (0.038) vs 2.621 (0.056); slope 0.336 (0.005) vs 0.282 (0.009) (Table 3).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Zhou, W., & Kim, Y. (2024). Innovative music education: An empirical assessment of ChatGPT-4's impact on student learning experiences. Education and Information Technologies, 29, 20855-20881 (outcome there: musical knowledge acquisition, not creativity).
sample_overlap.quote: These students were drawn from the cohort involved in our earlier study on the short-term effects of ChatGPT-4 (Zhou & Kim, 2024), thereby providing continuity for a follow-up investigation.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated; no specific funding (p. 17, Funding statement); authors declare no conflict of interest.

data_and_code.data_url: Available on request from the corresponding author (p. 17)

eligibility.reason: Criterion 2: 74 students analyzed (36 + 38, Table 6). Criterion 3: creativity of submitted music products rated by two blinded expert assessors while AI was available. Criterion 1 is unclear: the paper says participants were 'randomly assigned' but that assignment was 'conducted at the class level', does not state how many classes, and twice labels the design quasi-experimental (abstract; p. 5). If only one class per arm was randomized, this is an intact-class comparison (quasi_people/observational). Prior AI exposure also differs: the cohort comes from the earlier Zhou & Kim (2024) experiment, and the latent intercepts show the experimental group higher at Week 1 (3.281 vs 3.004).

one_line_finding: After 24 weeks, ChatGPT-4 supported music students scored higher on rater-scored creativity than traditionally taught students, adjusted means 4.71 (SE 0.18, n = 36) vs 4.35 (SE 0.17, n = 38), F(1, 69) = 7.216, p = .009, η² = .096 (Tables 5-6, p. 12), with steeper latent growth slopes, 0.315 vs 0.210 (Table 3, p. 9).
open_questions: How many classes were randomized, and which class went to which arm? The text says assignment was at the class level but gives no number.
Which time point (final week, mean of weeks, or another aggregation) is the dependent variable in the MANCOVA (Tables 4-6)? Not stated.

The text says baseline comparability was confirmed by multivariate and univariate tests 'see Tables 1 and 2', but Table 1 lists instructional themes and Table 2 reports growth-model fit; no baseline comparison table appears. The latent intercepts (Table 3) show the experimental group higher at the start.
Timeline wording varies: '24-week intervention' with '12 repeated measurement points' every two weeks, but Figs. 1-2 label the axis 'Week' 1-12, and RQ3/RQ4 refer to 'weeks 1 to 12' and 'week 12'.
Table 2 reports for the linear creativity model χ² = 885.330 on df = 78 (p < .000) together with RMSEA = .021; an auditor may wish to check this combination.
Adjusted means in Table 6 (4.71 vs 4.35) are far below the Fig. 1 end-point estimates (about 6.7 vs 5.3), consistent with the MANCOVA outcome not being the final-week score; the paper does not say.
notes: The candidate record guessed after_ai; the scored outputs were produced during the intervention with AI available to the experimental group, so the creativity outcome is with_ai. No outcome is measured after AI removal; the paper lists that as future research (p. 16). Not recorded as outcomes: the cross-lagged panel model (creativity-analysis paths, Table 7), the epistemic network analysis (Table 8, Fig. 3-4), and the Markov transition model (Figs. 5-6); these use interaction-log codes or within-construct dynamics, the ENA and Markov analyses cover the experimental group only (N = 36), and none is a creativity contrast between arms. Rubric scores are reported only as adjusted means with standard errors and latent growth parameters; no unadjusted arm means or standard deviations are printed. Same instructor taught both groups (p. 6).
